The film lasts only about 45 seconds: a magician winds up a human-shaped automaton, the figure grows, strikes back and is hammered down to doll size. For more than a century, viewers knew Georges Méliès’s “Gugusse and the Automaton” largely by reputation.

Now the 1897 trick short is streaming again after Library of Congress technicians identified a surviving print among roughly 10 battered nitrate reels and spent more than a week repairing, scanning and stabilizing it.

The recovery appears in the Library’s July–August magazine and National Screening Room catalog. The catalog lists the French Star Film production as probably photographed in 1897 and notes that the surviving digital copy ends abruptly but appears complete.

When the reels reached the National Audio-Visual Conservation Center in Culpeper, Virginia, some cans were rusted, some film had crumbled and other strips had fused together. Staff examined the material frame by frame rather than risk running it through a projector.

A black star on an automaton’s pedestal helped reveal what they had. The action matched a film listed as Star Film catalog number 111: Méliès, playing the magician Gugusse, confronts a Pierrot figure that begins as a mechanical doll and becomes an unruly human-sized opponent.

The Library describes it as the first screen appearance of what might be called a robot. That wording matters. The film predates the word “robot” by more than two decades, and its character draws on the older stage tradition of clockwork automatons.

The reels came from the family of William DeLyle Frisbee, a western Pennsylvania farmer and teacher who also traveled with early motion pictures. His great-grandson Bill McFarland eventually drove the inherited cache from Grand Rapids, Michigan, to the Library in September 2025.

The films had passed through basements, barns, garages and a small trunk. That chain was far from archival, but it kept material that could not safely be projected from being discarded. The cache also held another Méliès film from 1900 and fragments of an early Thomas Edison title.

The recovered “Gugusse” print is not the camera negative. The Library says it is a duplicate at least three generations removed from the original, evidence of the copying and circulation that helped some early films survive after their masters vanished.

Technicians repaired the fragile nitrate stock, scanned it and stabilized the digital image. The work took more than a week. It did not erase every scratch, flicker or missing edge; those marks document the physical history of the surviving copy.

Méliès made more than 500 films, but most original negatives disappeared. Some were melted for their silver and celluloid during World War I, and the filmmaker later burned more. About 300 titles are known to survive, according to the Library, which holds roughly 60.

The recovered short expands that record by less than a minute, yet its subject bridges two histories: Méliès’s experiments with cinematic illusion and the long cultural idea of artificial figures escaping human control.

Its new availability is also the final preservation step that matters to the public. The catalog entry includes a downloadable viewing copy and a rights note saying the Library knows of no U.S. copyright restriction on the vast majority of films in the collection. A work once accessible only as a title in film history can again be watched as a moving image.

articles.body:
The Library of Congress has turned 4,000 square feet on the ground floor of its Thomas Jefferson Building into a research room designed for a group that rarely gets its own federal reading space: children and teenagers.

The Source: Where Curiosity Sparks Discovery opened May 9 and is designed especially for visitors ages 8 to 15, along with families and school groups. A new July/August Library of Congress Magazine feature shows the finished gallery and explains how its interactive stations are meant to make research feel like an active hunt rather than a formal assignment.

The room's most recognizable object is an animated card catalog. Opening its drawers can trigger collection-based scenes, including the tornado from The Wizard of Oz, a rocket launch and Rosa Parks' pancake recipe. The device uses the shape of an old research tool to introduce material held in many formats.

Elsewhere, seven Library staff members appear in short videos at a research desk, describing their work and suggesting items to explore. A large digital Source Book lets visitors assemble and share a collage from collection images, making their own trail through what they found.

The Library says the room contains hundreds of digitized and replica items spanning image, film, sound and text collections. The use of reproductions is important: young visitors can manipulate and compare material without putting fragile originals at risk.

The Source also treats research as a conversation. Staff and volunteers run scheduled Source Spotlight demonstrations, and a free Source Guide gives families a structure for a self-directed visit. The Library recommends allowing 30 to 45 minutes, though the gallery is built to support different paths rather than one fixed sequence.

The design was not produced only for young people; children helped shape it. The Library convened a youth advisory council of about two dozen children ages 8 to 12 in fall 2021. They reacted to early designs, tested ideas and offered blunt feedback about what felt inviting.

Weston Moats, one of those advisers, is pictured in the magazine feature inside the completed gallery. The visible result is a room with saturated orange fixtures, large-scale media and many points of entry—an environment that presents federal collections without mimicking an adult reading room.

The gallery is free, but visiting rules still apply. Children under 16 must remain with an adult. During Washington's summer and other school breaks, public hours are Tuesday through Friday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. During the school year, weekday public hours begin at 1 p.m.; Saturday hours remain 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

School and organized groups can use workshop programs or request free timed-entry tickets for visits during public hours. The Source is immediately to the right of the Jefferson Building's main entrance on the ground floor.

The new room does not make every part of Library research child-accessible, and its displays rely on selected digitized or replica objects rather than open access to the full physical collection. Its more consequential experiment is narrower: whether a national library can teach primary-source habits—asking questions, comparing formats and tracing evidence—before visitors think of research as something reserved for specialists.

Unemployment rates moved in opposite directions across nearly equal numbers of U.S. metropolitan areas in June, while statistically significant payroll growth remained concentrated in a small group of local economies, federal data released Wednesday show.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that jobless rates were higher than a year earlier in 184 of 387 metropolitan areas, lower in 178 and unchanged in 25. The national unemployment rate was 4.4 percent on a not-seasonally-adjusted basis, the same as in June 2025.

The payroll figures were considerably less balanced. Nonfarm employment increased significantly over the year in 15 metropolitan areas and decreased in three, while BLS classified the remaining 369 as essentially unchanged. BLS cites metro payroll changes in its release only when they are statistically significant at the 90 percent confidence level.

Dallas-Fort Worth-Arlington recorded the largest numerical payroll gain, adding 54,600 jobs from June 2025. Las Vegas-Henderson-North Las Vegas added 33,500, while Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler added 33,200. Athens-Clarke County, Georgia, posted the largest percentage increase at 4.1 percent.

The largest loss was in Washington-Arlington-Alexandria, where payroll employment fell by 83,500, or 2.4 percent. Portland-Vancouver-Hillsboro lost 25,700 jobs, or 2.1 percent, and Bloomington, Indiana, lost 3,300, or 4.2 percent.

Sioux Falls, South Dakota-Minnesota, had the lowest metro unemployment rate at 1.9 percent, followed by Rapid City, South Dakota, at 2.0 percent. El Centro, California, had the highest rate at 17.6 percent.

Lake Havasu City-Kingman, Arizona, recorded the largest year-over-year increase in its unemployment rate, rising 1.7 percentage points. Kokomo, Indiana, posted the largest decline, falling 1.9 percentage points.

The unemployment and payroll figures come from different BLS programs and measure different things. Unemployment estimates describe people by where they live, while payroll estimates count jobs by where establishments are located. Both sets of metro figures in the release are not seasonally adjusted.

The latest estimates remain subject to revision. BLS said it plans to publish preliminary benchmark revisions for March 2026 on Aug. 28, using employment counts derived from unemployment-insurance tax records. Final benchmark revisions for state and metropolitan series are scheduled with the January 2027 data release.

NASA-funded researchers will chase the August 12 total solar eclipse with a high-altitude jet and launch 86 scientific balloons from Iceland and Spain, turning the Moon’s shadow into a coordinated solar and atmospheric experiment.

The eclipse crosses Greenland, Iceland and Spain. A NASA WB-57 will fly along the path at about 460 miles per hour and 50,000 feet, above most clouds and much of the atmosphere that absorbs infrared light before it reaches ground telescopes.

Four cameras in the aircraft’s nose will record at least 20 images per second in multiple visible and infrared wavelengths. Scientists plan to examine fast-changing structures in the solar corona, suspended prominences and the relationship between coronal material and the solar wind.

Chasing the shadow extends the observation window. NASA says the longest view of the corona from the ground will be two minutes and 18 seconds, while the aircraft should remain in totality for nearly three minutes. That extra time produces more frames of a phenomenon that cannot be paused or repeated.

The instrument, called the SCIFLI Multispectral Airborne Imager, also flew during the April 2024 eclipse. The team adjusted exposure plans after bright features were overexposed in some earlier imagery and will use newer processing software to analyze the 2026 data sooner.

The balloon campaign targets a different layer of the event. In Iceland, two university teams plan to launch 80 balloons beginning 18 hours before totality and continuing until eight hours afterward, measuring how sudden darkness changes the atmospheric boundary layer near Earth’s surface.

Earlier eclipse campaigns found that the boundary layer thinned under clear skies but not cloudy ones. Iceland’s long August daylight creates a distinct test because its brief night may produce a weaker ordinary nighttime transition than researchers observed in 2023 and 2024.

In Spain, three teams plan six balloons with 360-degree cameras and ozone instruments. Ozone requires sunlight to form, and similar instruments measured a decline during the 2024 eclipse; the later time of day and different season give researchers another set of conditions to compare.

The flight and balloon counts are plans, not completed observations. Weather, launch conditions and aircraft operations can change them, and the scientific claims will come only after calibration and analysis. The experiment’s immediate news is its design: one brief shadow sampled across altitude, wavelength, geography and time.

NASA says the longest view of the corona from the ground will be two minutes and 18 seconds, while the aircraft should remain in totality for nearly three minutes. That extra time produces more frames of a phenomenon that cannot be paused or repeated.

The instrument, called the SCIFLI Multispectral Airborne Imager, also flew during the April 2024 eclipse. The team adjusted exposure plans after bright features were overexposed in some earlier imagery and will use newer processing software to analyze the 2026 data sooner.

The balloon campaign targets a different layer of the event. In Iceland, two university teams plan to launch 80 balloons beginning 18 hours before totality and continuing until eight hours afterward, measuring how sudden darkness changes the atmospheric boundary layer near Earth’s surface.

bodyBlocks.alt: Graphic compares 80 balloons in Iceland with six camera and ozone balloons in Spain.
bodyBlocks.caption: Student teams will test how sudden darkness changes the atmospheric boundary layer and ozone.
bodyBlocks.credit: Boho News graphic from NASA eclipse plan

bodyBlocks.text: Earlier eclipse campaigns found that the boundary layer thinned under clear skies but not cloudy ones. Iceland’s long August daylight creates a distinct test because its brief night may produce a weaker ordinary nighttime transition than researchers observed in 2023 and 2024.

In Spain, three teams plan six balloons with 360-degree cameras and ozone instruments. Ozone requires sunlight to form, and similar instruments measured a decline during the 2024 eclipse; the later time of day and different season give researchers another set of conditions to compare.

The flight and balloon counts are plans, not completed observations. Weather, launch conditions and aircraft operations can change them, and the scientific claims will come only after calibration and analysis. The experiment’s immediate news is its design: one brief shadow sampled across altitude, wavelength, geography and time.

articles.body:
NASA has opened a 25,000-square-foot wind-tunnel facility in Virginia that can suspend free-flying models in a 20-foot-wide vertical column of air moving as fast as 117 miles per hour.

The Flight Dynamics Research Facility began operating July 31 at Langley Research Center in Hampton. NASA describes it as the agency’s first major new wind tunnel in more than 40 years and a replacement for two aging facilities that shaped decades of aircraft and spacecraft testing.

Its purpose is not simply to push air past a fixed wing. Researchers can mount models on test equipment or let them fly freely inside the chamber, then study stability, spins, control, parachutes and the behavior of vehicles descending through an atmosphere.

The vertical test chamber is 20 feet in diameter, giving air more room to flow around larger and more detailed models. NASA says that improves the quality of measurements and expands the class of free-flight experiments the tunnel can handle.

Its maximum airspeed is twice that of the facilities it replaces. At 117 mph, researchers can fly heavier scale models and simulate some full-scale vehicles at higher altitude, where thinner air changes the relationship among size, speed and aerodynamic force.

The speed figure is a facility limit, not a claim that every test will run at the maximum. Researchers need controlled, repeatable airflow, and many questions about slow-speed stability or parachute behavior require lower settings.

The airflow comes from four 750-horsepower motors. Each drives a 14-foot-diameter fan with eight carbon-fiber blades, for 32 blades across the wind system and 3,000 horsepower of installed motor rating.

NASA says the lightweight blades allow the system to change airspeed quickly and precisely during free-flight work. That responsiveness matters when a model moves through the chamber and researchers need to keep it inside a safe test envelope.

The tunnel can support aircraft-safety studies, experimental X-planes, drones and autonomous vehicles. Its spaceflight work is atmospheric: models of reentry capsules, parachutes and landing systems, along with possible aircraft for Mars or other worlds with atmospheres.

Those uses are capabilities, not completed results. NASA’s opening announcement does not identify a first research campaign or publish validation data from a specific vehicle.

The new facility combines and improves the roles of Langley’s 20-Foot Vertical Spin Tunnel and 12-Foot Low-Speed Tunnel. The spin tunnel opened in 1941 and became a specialized place to study how aircraft enter and recover from spins; the smaller low-speed tunnel supported free-flight and control research.

Bringing their work into one modern building is meant to reduce maintenance demands and give research teams digital systems and a flexible test space. It is the fourth building delivered through NASA’s long-term Langley partnership with the General Services Administration.

That campus story is important because wind tunnels are infrastructure. Their scientific value depends on calibration, repeatability, model preparation, sensors and the ability to run safely over years—not on opening-day dimensions alone.

The next evidence will come from actual campaigns: what vehicles use the chamber, whether the airflow and controls perform as specified, and what designs change because of the measurements. The opening supplies the tool; experiments will supply the findings.

articles.body:
Four commercial lunar landers are moving through assembly and ground tests as NASA tries to turn a sequence of one-off Moon missions into a repeatable cargo network. The most important word in that sentence is “tries”: none of the milestones NASA detailed Tuesday is a completed delivery.

NASA’s Aug. 4 update says Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines and Voyager Technologies are working toward lander flights by 2028. The agency’s first phase, running through 2029, calls for more than 20 robotic landings, with successive missions testing systems and placing instruments before additional human operations near the lunar south pole.

The update supplies an unusually useful snapshot of what is actually built, what is being tested and what still has to happen. It also shows why a launch target should not be confused with a delivery: each vehicle still faces integration, environmental or propulsion work before it can leave Earth.

Blue Origin’s uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1, named Endurance, completed an environmental campaign in NASA Johnson’s Thermal Vacuum Chamber A. The chamber recreated vacuum and extreme temperatures so engineers could evaluate structural and thermal performance before launch.

NASA says the lander’s structure, propulsion elements and avionics are fully assembled. It has completed communications checkouts with the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System and Deep Space Network. The next major test NASA identified is loading cryogenic propellants.

Endurance is intended to demonstrate precision landing, cryogenic propulsion and autonomous guidance, navigation and control. NASA has assigned two payloads: cameras to observe how the engine plume interacts with lunar soil and a laser retroreflector that orbiting spacecraft can use for precise position measurements.

Firefly’s Blue Ghost Mission 2 pairs a lander with the Elytra orbital spacecraft in a stack NASA says is 22 feet tall—nearly three times the height of the company’s first Blue Ghost vehicle. The mission is planned for the Moon’s far side and is slated to carry three NASA payloads. Far-side operations also require a communications architecture that does not depend on a direct line to Earth.

Intuitive Machines’ third Nova-C lander, named Trinity, is being assembled alongside Altus-1, the company’s first lunar data-relay satellite. NASA says long-duration thermal-vacuum work on descent sensors is complete; engine integration and hot-fire testing remain. The planned manifest includes three payloads on Altus-1 and, on the surface, five NASA payloads, six commercial payloads and one civil payload.

Voyager’s Griffin-1 is undergoing environmental testing at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. NASA says the vehicle recently completed mass-properties testing, data needed for guidance, navigation, control and flight-dynamics models. The lander is planned to carry Astrolab’s FLIP rover with five NASA payloads, then return to Pittsburgh for final assembly after the JPL campaign.

NASA is also working with Northrop Grumman on three surface technology demonstrations derived from power and avionics hardware developed for Gateway’s HALO module. The demonstrations are meant to test survival through long cold periods, shared surface power and supporting avionics.

Those details matter because landing is only the first engineering problem. A durable lunar logistics system has to move payloads, communicate around terrain and the far side, distribute power and keep hardware alive through darkness and temperature swings.

NASA’s schedule remains a planning framework. Launch licensing, integration, test results, launch-provider readiness and lunar conditions can all move individual missions. The concrete news in the Aug. 4 update is the hardware status: one large cargo lander has completed thermal-vacuum testing, another is stacked with an orbiter, a third is in assembly and a fourth is in environmental tests.

articles.body:
A NASA mission designed to watch the solar wind continuously has passed its first forecasting test: researchers used PUNCH imagery to predict when a coronal mass ejection would reach near-Earth space, and the estimate missed by less than 30 minutes.

That is a striking improvement over the roughly five-hour arrival window NASA says current methods provide. It is also one retrospective proof of concept—not yet an operational forecasting system and not yet a peer-reviewed result.

NASA announced the analysis Aug. 4 after researchers presented it at the Committee on Space Research Scientific Meeting. The work is under review at the journal Space Weather. Those qualifications matter because the result comes from a single eruption whose actual arrival was already known when the team tested its method.

Coronal mass ejections are large expulsions of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun. Their effects can disturb satellites, radio links, navigation systems and electric-power infrastructure, but the severity depends on more than arrival time. Direction, speed and the magnetic orientation of the ejected material also matter.

Before PUNCH, NASA says coronagraphs could directly follow an ejection through roughly the first fifth of its trip to Earth. Forecasters then had to infer how the cloud changed across much of the remaining distance.

PUNCH—short for Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere—uses four small spacecraft in low Earth orbit to make continuous three-dimensional observations of the inner solar system. Its combined field of view can track solar eruptions nearly to Earth and produce a new image every four minutes.

Researchers revisited a coronal mass ejection that left the Sun on May 31, 2025. They fed PUNCH images into a basic computer model that followed the eruption’s leading edge and used changes in speed and geometry to calculate an arrival time.

Twelve hours after the eruption left the Sun, the model’s estimate stabilized. It predicted arrival eight hours later. NASA says the final estimate was accurate to within half an hour—about 10 times tighter than the five-hour window associated with the currently used approach.

The model also indicated when its answer had stabilized. That is operationally important: a forecast is more useful when forecasters can tell whether the estimate is still moving or has become dependable enough to support planning.

The first test does not establish a general 30-minute error rate. Coronal mass ejections differ in shape, speed, direction and interaction with the ambient solar wind. A method that performs well on one event can fail on a different geometry.

Researchers will need to repeat the analysis across many eruptions, compare it against independent forecasting methods and complete peer review. Operational forecasters would also have to evaluate data latency, spacecraft coverage, model reliability and failure modes.

The imagery is already yielding scientific information beyond timing. NASA says the observations show more internal structure than earlier views, including clumpy material that continues to evolve as it crosses the solar system. That can improve models of how plasma moves not only around the Sun but in other astrophysical settings.

The honest reading is therefore two-part: PUNCH demonstrated that continuous imaging can sharply improve one arrival estimate, and the mission has not yet demonstrated that performance across the range of storms a real forecast service must handle.

NASA is targeting Aug. 30 for the launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, moving the wide-field infrared observatory from final ground processing toward a five-year survey mission.

The agency lists liftoff for 7:26 a.m. EDT on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. As with any launch, the date and time remain subject to technical readiness, weather and range decisions.

After launch, Roman will travel to a quasi-halo orbit around the second Sun–Earth Lagrange point, or L2. That location keeps the Sun and Earth in roughly the same direction from the spacecraft, supporting stable observations and thermal conditions far beyond low Earth orbit.

Roman’s 2.4-meter primary mirror is the same diameter as Hubble’s, but the missions are built for different survey scales. Roman’s 288-megapixel Wide Field Instrument will capture near-infrared images with Hubble-like sharpness across a field at least 100 times larger, according to NASA.

That combination is intended to turn deep, detailed observations into panoramic surveys. Roman’s core science includes measuring the growth and expansion history of the universe, mapping matter across cosmic time and finding planets through gravitational microlensing.

A second instrument, the Coronagraph Instrument technology demonstration, will suppress starlight to test high-contrast imaging of nearby planets and debris disks. NASA describes it as a demonstration of techniques for future missions, not the primary engine of Roman’s wide-field surveys.

The expanded field creates a data problem as well as a science opportunity. NASA’s technical overview projects about 11 terabits of data per day, while the mission FAQ says the observations will enter a public archive with no proprietary period.

That access policy means multiple teams can analyze the same observations without waiting through an exclusive-use window. It also increases the importance of processing pipelines, searchable archives and computing resources capable of handling the mission’s survey volume.

Roman’s primary mission is approximately five years. The observatory is being designed to support another five years, but an extension will depend on spacecraft health, fuel and future operating decisions rather than the launch schedule alone.

The Aug. 30 target marks the point when years of assembly and testing become a launch campaign. If Roman reaches L2 and completes commissioning, its defining capability will not be a single image: it will be the repeated, public, wide-field record needed to measure how large populations of galaxies, stars and planets change across the sky.

bodyBlocks.text: NASA is targeting Aug. 30 for the launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, moving the wide-field infrared observatory from final ground processing toward a five-year survey mission.

The agency lists liftoff for 7:26 a.m. EDT on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. As with any launch, the date and time remain subject to technical readiness, weather and range decisions.

After launch, Roman will travel to a quasi-halo orbit around the second Sun–Earth Lagrange point, or L2. That location keeps the Sun and Earth in roughly the same direction from the spacecraft, supporting stable observations and thermal conditions far beyond low Earth orbit.

bodyBlocks.text: Roman’s 2.4-meter primary mirror is the same diameter as Hubble’s, but the missions are built for different survey scales. A second instrument, the Coronagraph Instrument technology demonstration, will suppress starlight to test high-contrast imaging of nearby planets and debris disks. NASA describes it as a demonstration of techniques for future missions, not the primary engine of Roman’s wide-field surveys.

NASA has scheduled three U.S. spacewalks for Aug. 6, Aug. 13 and Aug. 25, a compact run of outside work that links the International Space Station's day-to-day upkeep with two longer-term priorities: adding power and preparing the complex for its eventual deorbit.

The first operation is the most fully specified. NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Anil Menon are due to leave the Quest airlock Aug. 6. Coverage begins at 7 a.m. EDT, and NASA expects the spacewalk to begin at 8:35 a.m. and last about six and a half hours.

Meir and Menon are assigned to install hardware on the station's 3B power channel. The modification is intended to prepare that channel for a seventh International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array, or IROSA, which NASA says is scheduled for delivery later in 2026.

The pairing mixes deep spacewalk experience with a debut. This will be Meir's sixth spacewalk and Menon's first. Meir will wear the suit marked with red stripes as crew member 1; Menon will wear the unmarked suit as crew member 2.

NASA's second August outing, U.S. spacewalk 97 on Aug. 13, is aimed at communications. Two astronauts will replace a Space-to-Ground antenna, part of the system used to move data and high-speed communications between the station and Mission Control in Houston. NASA has not yet announced the crew or timing.

The Aug. 25 operation combines cabling and docking work. The crew for U.S. spacewalk 98 is expected to connect power-channel cables and data-relay systems, work NASA describes as part of continuing maintenance and preparation for the station's future deorbit. The astronauts also are scheduled to replace a navigational aid on the forward port of the Harmony module, where visiting spacecraft dock.

NASA counts the three outings as the 281st, 282nd and 283rd spacewalks conducted for station assembly, maintenance and upgrades. That sequence is more than a milestone: it shows how the station's final era still demands new infrastructure.

IROSA panels are smaller than the station's original arrays but use more efficient cells. Earlier units were mounted in front of portions of the legacy arrays, adding generation while using existing tracking and power-distribution hardware. NASA says the next array will add power needed for critical operations, including a safe, controlled deorbit.

The schedule remains partly provisional. NASA said it will publish the assigned crews, start times and coverage details for the Aug. 13 and Aug. 25 spacewalks closer to those dates. Operational timing can also move as station managers assess equipment, crew readiness and conditions aboard the orbiting laboratory.

articles.body:
A soccer ball that Pelé presented to President Gerald Ford in 1975 is the centerpiece of a new temporary display at the National Archives Museum in Washington.

“The Beautiful Game” runs from July 6 through August 19 in the museum’s West Rotunda Gallery. The compact exhibit connects one object to a moment when Pelé’s arrival in the North American Soccer League was helping draw new attention to the sport in the United States.

Pelé visited the White House on June 28, 1975, while the New York Cosmos were in Washington to play the Washington Diplomats. In the Rose Garden, Ford tried juggling the ball as Pelé watched, and official White House photographers preserved the exchange.

The ball itself carries another layer of local history: players from the 1975 Washington Diplomats signed it. The Archives’ exhibit page does not identify every signature, so the object should be read as a team artifact rather than a complete roster key.

Pelé had joined the Cosmos earlier that year after a celebrated career with Santos and Brazil. His U.S. appearances became cultural events as well as matches, drawing political leaders and people who had rarely followed professional soccer.

The Ford visit is part of a broader presidential record in the Archives. Photographs also show Pelé autographing a ball for President Richard Nixon in 1973, meeting President Jimmy Carter in 1977 and joining President Ronald Reagan and Brazilian President José Sarney at a 1986 state dinner.

Those images are not interchangeable with the exhibit object. The displayed ball is tied specifically to the 1975 Cosmos trip, the Washington Diplomats signatures and Ford’s Rose Garden exchange. The other photographs document how Pelé’s public role extended across administrations.

The National Archives preserves presidential photographs and objects as federal records, allowing the public to trace not only official policy but the cultural diplomacy surrounding athletes, artists and visiting figures.

For visitors, the useful detail is the short window. The ball is scheduled to remain on view through August 19, after which the temporary display closes. The National Archives Museum lists admission as free, with timed-entry reservations recommended.

articles.body:
The Library of Congress is turning its annual book festival into a broader one-day culture program this month, bringing more than 80 authors to Washington while adding film, music, recorded sound, veterans’ history and American folklife to the usual author conversations.

The 26th National Book Festival is scheduled for Saturday, Aug. 22, at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center. The event runs from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., with doors opening at 8:30. Admission remains free, but the Library says a free entry ticket will be required for the first time; individual sessions do not require separate tickets.

That ticket change is the practical detail most likely to surprise returning visitors. The Library’s July lineup announcement directs attendees to reserve entry through the festival site rather than simply arriving at the building.

The announced lineup includes actor and memoirist Cynthia Erivo, director Martin Scorsese, comedian and middle-grade author Kate McKinnon, novelist Ann Patchett and U.S. Poet Laureate Arthur Sze. The point is not merely celebrity: the program uses their appearances to connect new books with the Library’s holdings in film, sound and literature.

Scorsese is scheduled to discuss filmmaking and preservation while showing selected clips. Patchett, the 2026 recipient of the Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction, is due to discuss her novel “Whistler.” Sze’s program is tied to both his signature poet-laureate project and a guide to poetry in translation.

Those are only the top-line names. The Library’s release lists fiction, nonfiction, biography, history, memoir, poetry, translation, young-adult, middle-grade and picture-book authors. It describes the figure as more than 80 authors rather than a final attendance count, and published lineups can change before an event.

The festival site says a selection of programs will be livestreamed. The July announcement is more specific: Main Stage events are due to stream through loc.gov/bookfest. Videos of presentations are expected to appear on the Library’s site and YouTube channel after the festival.

That distinction matters for remote viewers. “Livestreamed” does not mean every room will be available in real time. The Library promises on-demand video later, but it does not provide a release time for each recording.

Beyond stages and signing lines, the Library says the festival will include a Story District, a STEM District, a Workshop Space and the Roadmap to Reading area. The design turns the convention floor into a set of different ways to encounter books: listening, making, experimenting and browsing work tied to states and territories.

The event is also part of the Library’s America 250 programming. That framing expands the festival into the institution’s film, music, veterans’ history and folklife collections, but it does not make the day a single historical program. The published roster still ranges across contemporary fiction, memoir, poetry and books for younger readers.

The date, venue, public hours, door time, free admission and ticket requirement are all stated in current Library records. The lineup announcement identifies more than 80 authors and says the Main Stage will be livestreamed.

Session times, room assignments and participant availability remain operational details. Anyone building a personal schedule should use the live festival page close to Aug. 22 rather than rely on a saved program or an early announcement.

The durable story is the scale and shape of the event: one free, ticketed day in downtown Washington, more than 80 authors, and a Library of Congress program that now treats books as an entry point to film, recorded sound, music, history and hands-on learning.

National Park Week will run Aug. 22 through Aug. 30, with a fee-free day for U.S. residents on Aug. 25 marking the National Park Service’s 110th birthday.

The nine-day observance begins with National Junior Ranger Day on Aug. 22 and includes guided tours, educational exhibits and local programs under the theme “Celebrate America’s Story,” according to the Park Service.

The Aug. 25 waiver applies to entrance fees at Park Service sites that normally charge them. It does not automatically eliminate timed-entry or tour reservations, and visitors should not assume camping, lodging, parking, special-use or other activity fees are included.

The Park Service notes that most of its sites do not charge an entrance fee. At fee-charging parks, visitors normally need a standard pass, a park-specific annual pass or an America the Beautiful interagency pass.

The birthday waiver is limited to U.S. residents. The agency’s current pass table separately lists an $80 resident annual pass for U.S. citizens and residents and a $250 nonresident annual pass.

A free-entrance day also does not guarantee entry. Some high-traffic parks use timed vehicle entry or require reservations for tours, buildings or natural features. Those reservations are typically handled through Recreation.gov and can become available on a rolling basis.

The 433-unit National Park System includes landscapes, battlefields, monuments and historic buildings. The week’s framing ties the service’s birthday to the 250th anniversary of American independence.

Programs differ by park. The national announcement does not create one universal schedule, so the practical source for hours, closures, weather, road conditions and local events remains each park’s own current-conditions page.

Visitors planning around Aug. 25 should check both whether a destination normally charges an entrance fee and whether it requires a reservation. A pass or fee waiver covers access costs; it does not replace a scarce entry slot.

National Park Week ends Aug. 30. The Park Service says hundreds of activities are planned nationally, but it has not published a single final attendance estimate or consolidated count of every local event.

articles.body:
NCAA baseball committees have proposed allowing ball-strike challenges and in-game bat sensors next season while limiting electronic offensive communication, a package that would put more technology into some decisions and less into signal delivery.

In Division I, teams could use a ball-strike challenge system when the technology is available during regular-season and postseason games. Divisions II and III could seek approval to test the system under an experimental rule.

The Southeastern Conference tested pitch challenges during its May tournament. The NCAA announcement does not specify a single vendor, camera configuration or installation standard, so availability could differ across venues.

Bat sensor technology would become permissible for in-game data collection in all divisions under the proposal. Division I programs have experimented with sensors for the past two seasons.

The committees drew a boundary around real-time communication. Division I teams would no longer be allowed to use electronic devices to send offensive signals to players before a pitch, reflecting concern that direct instructions could create an unfair advantage.

The proposals also reshape the field. Teams could use 18-inch square bases next season while the existing 15-inch base remains standard, and a double first base would be required for all games.

Offensive conferences would increase to six, allowing a batter to request a reset of the action clock. A coach could participate in no more than three charged offensive conferences, with one additional conference in extra innings.

Division I would add a 30-second timer between batters, during mound visits and during offensive timeouts. Video review could expand to certain fair-or-foul decisions and tag plays regardless of field location.

None of those recommendations is final yet. The Division II and III Playing Rules Oversight Panel is scheduled to review the package August 11, and the Division I Baseball Oversight Committee is scheduled for August 24.

The votes will determine whether the 2026–27 rulebook adopts the committees’ balance: automated assistance for narrowly defined calls, more permitted performance data and a tighter prohibition on technology that can direct offense in real time.

articles.body:
NCAA Division I plans to move incoming athletes to an age-based eligibility model beginning with the fall 2027 class, replacing many sport-specific season limits, redshirt rules and extension waivers with a five-year period tied to enrollment age.

Under the Cabinet-approved model, a student can receive up to five years of eligibility if full-time college enrollment begins no later than the academic year after the student’s 19th birthday. The rule changes how the period is defined; it does not promise five seasons to every athlete regardless of enrollment history.

The transition separates three groups. Prospects first enrolling full time in fall 2027 or later use only the age model. Students first enrolling during 2026–27 and current athletes with eligibility remaining after 2025–26 use either the old four-seasons-in-five-years framework or the new model, whichever is more favorable.

Athletes who used their final season under the prior rules during 2025–26 do not receive another season through the transition. That boundary prevents the change from reopening eligibility for everyone whose previous clock already ended.

The Cabinet listed pregnancy, active-duty military service and official religious missions as circumstances that can delay or pause the age-based period. The exception applies only when the student does not participate in organized competition during that time, and the NCAA Eligibility Center will administer it.

The new model also removes waivers under the age system, including clock extensions and waivers formerly used for hardship, season-of-competition or delayed-enrollment cases. Legacy waiver requests based on circumstances through 2025–26 had a July 31 submission deadline.

For schools, the change reduces the number of sport-specific calculations but makes age and first full-time enrollment central compliance facts. Roster planning during the transition will require schools to evaluate both systems for eligible current athletes rather than automatically applying only the new one.

The NCAA’s June 23 page states that the Cabinet voted unanimously and presents the change as adopted, while also noting that the action was not final until the meeting concluded the next day. The public record does not describe a later reversal, but that drafting caveat belongs in the implementation record.

The practical question for any athlete is therefore individual: date of birth, first full-time enrollment, participation history, and whether eligibility remained after 2025–26. The broad five-year description cannot replace a school’s fact-specific eligibility determination.

articles.body:
NCAA Division III has amended its reinstatement guidance to allow immediate penalty reductions for a narrow group of first-time sports-betting violations tied to clinical evaluation and support.

Three conditions define the pathway. The conduct must be the student-athlete’s first betting violation, it cannot raise game-integrity concerns, and the athlete must complete a clinical evaluation and receive related support.

That structure is not blanket amnesty. A first violation involving manipulation, inside information or another integrity concern does not fit the announced pathway, and a later violation is outside the first-offense condition.

The Management Council said the amendment is intended to encourage student-athletes to seek help while preserving the association’s responsibility to protect competition. Linking relief to evaluation distinguishes a treatment-oriented response from simply reducing every penalty.

The public announcement describes eligibility for possible immediate reductions, not an automatic outcome in every case. Reinstatement still depends on the facts submitted and the NCAA process, and the page does not identify or decide any individual athlete’s case.

Sports-betting rules operate alongside state gambling laws and team policies, but those systems answer different questions. Division III reinstatement governs eligibility in NCAA competition; it does not erase a wager, settle a state-law issue or provide individualized health advice.

The council took other governance actions at the same meeting. It sponsored 2027 legislation to establish a Division III flag football championship. If all three divisions adopt the proposal, a championship committee could begin work in January and the first tournament could be held in spring 2028.

Those dates remain conditional. Sponsorship starts the legislative process; it does not itself create the championship. The council’s 2027 and 2028 budgets and a new strategic plan also still required final approval from the Division III Presidents Council in August.

The betting amendment is the action with the most immediate athlete-facing effect. Its line is deliberate: treatment and a first violation can support reduced consequences, but integrity concerns remain disqualifying rather than negotiable.

articles.body:
Cut-resistant protective equipment will become mandatory for NCAA Division I men's hockey and National Collegiate women's hockey players beginning with the 2027-28 season, the association announced.

Players currently have the option to wear the equipment. During the 2026-27 academic year, the NCAA is encouraging protection designed for the neck, wrist and ankle areas before the requirement takes effect.

The rule does not yet apply to Division III. Members of the Division II and III Playing Rules Oversight Panel supported sending the proposal out for comment, and the Division III panel is expected to act on it at a September meeting.

The NCAA announcement did not identify approved brands or publish a complete product specification. Schools and equipment managers will need later guidance on standards, certification and enforcement before the mandatory season begins.

The association also approved a clarification allowing audio-communication devices and health-and-safety tracking technology in the bench area for all NCAA hockey. Video may not be used for coaching purposes on the bench.

Other changes arrive sooner. Division I men's hockey will add a trapezoid behind the net in 2026-27, limiting where goalkeepers may play the puck below the goal line. Division III men are scheduled to add the marking in 2027-28.

Regular-season overtime remains five minutes of three-on-three play for both men's and women's hockey. Women's conferences will determine whether a shootout follows a tie, including rules for nonconference and neutral-site games.

Additional approved changes allow defensive-zone hand passes, require both men's faceoff players to place their stick blades flat before the puck drop and restrict timeouts by a Division I men's team that is not allowed to change players after certain stoppages.

The cut-resistant equipment rule is the clearest player-safety change in the package. Its delayed effective date gives programs time to obtain compliant gear and allows Division III to finish its separate governance process.

articles.body:
NCAA men’s lacrosse is getting a wider replay rulebook. All three divisions approved new grounds for coaches to challenge goals, broader authority for officials to examine head and neck contact, and a shift from four-minute to 15-minute sudden-death overtime periods.

A coach may ask for review when a goal could be erased because the scoring team was offsides, had too many players on the field, or the player carrying the ball stepped on the midline or a restraining line. Those are defined triggers, not a general invitation to replay every disputed possession.

Timing controls the challenge. The possible violation must have happened within 15 seconds of the goal, and no whistle can sound between the violation and the score. If the game clock is not embedded in the video, officials may use a stopwatch while watching the play at actual speed.

Officials also receive separate authority involving player safety. They may initiate a review of possible contact to the head or neck even when no penalty was called on the field. When officials did call such a penalty, they may rescind it if replay confirms there was no illegal contact.

The combination expands review in two directions: coaches can test specific sequence violations that precede a goal, while officials can revisit a narrow safety issue. The NCAA announcement does not authorize an unlimited correction system for routine judgment calls.

Overtime remains sudden death, but its structure changes sharply. Instead of repeating four-minute periods and switching ends, teams will play 15-minute periods until a winning goal. Timeout and video-challenge rules remain unchanged during overtime.

A separate visibility change starts as a recommendation. Fluorescent green or yellow balls are recommended for the 2026–27 academic year and become mandatory in 2027–28. The NCAA said brighter colors should improve visibility for players, officials, spectators and television audiences.

The rules package also creates a fall experiment aimed at end-of-clock heaves from the defensive end. Participating teams may treat a release from below the defensive restraining line as a legitimate shot only if it becomes a goal or hits the goal frame.

For coaches, the immediate operational task is precise: preserve usable video, identify the triggering violation, and establish the 15-second sequence without an intervening whistle. For viewers, the most visible changes will be longer overtime segments and, eventually, brighter game balls.

articles.body:
NCAA men’s and women’s soccer coaches will receive two video challenges per game in 2026–27, replacing a review structure that relied more heavily on officials to decide when to look again.

The rule applies in games where video review is available. Each coach may challenge at any point, but the maximum remains two; the NCAA announcement does not describe a retained challenge after a successful review.

Official-initiated review becomes more limited during the first 80 minutes. Referees may independently check only clock questions and whether the ball crossed the goal line, leaving other allowable review issues to a coach’s challenge.

The final 10 minutes and overtime create a different balance. Officials may initiate review of any allowable play, but only when a team has exhausted its challenges. If a team still has a challenge, the coach must decide whether to use it.

The NCAA said the design is intended to improve accuracy without sacrificing pace. It makes the challenge inventory part of match strategy while preserving a late safety valve after that inventory is gone.

A separate goalkeeper rule changes both time and punishment. A goalkeeper will have eight seconds to release the ball after gaining possession, up from six, while officials visibly count the final five seconds.

Failure to release within eight seconds gives the opponent a corner kick. Under the previous rule, a six-second violation produced an indirect free kick. The NCAA said the change aligns college play with international rules.

The package also permits broader substitution timing in several divisions, allows video match officials in Division I games using review, mandates a fourth official in Division I and sets a three-hour weather-delay framework with conference oversight.

The most consequential replay change is not simply the number two. It is the sequence of authority: coaches control most review requests, officials retain narrow early powers, and broader late intervention returns only after a team has spent its challenges.

articles.body:
A fixed set of artificial-intelligence guardrails cannot be universally robust against adaptive adversarial prompts, according to a mathematical argument published by a senior National Institute of Standards and Technology scientist.

The finding is about a limit, not a declaration that AI security is impossible. Apostol Vassilev’s paper argues that when behavior is constrained by a finite rule system, a sufficiently adaptive adversary can construct inputs that expose cases the rules do not settle as intended.

NIST connects that argument to the logic of Kurt Gödel’s incompleteness theorems. The analogy does not mean a language model is a formal proof system in every respect; it is used to show why a finite compliance scheme should not be treated as permanently complete.

The operational consequence is a shift away from “one and done” security. NIST says organizations should continuously red-team systems to uncover new adversarial prompts, update defenses as those failures are found, and build resilience that limits impact and accelerates recovery.

That sequence changes what readiness means. Passing a pre-release evaluation establishes how a system behaved against the tests available at that moment. It does not establish that future users or attackers cannot discover a new interaction that bypasses the same controls.

Continuous monitoring also requires evidence, not merely a recurring calendar task. Teams need documented failure cases, reproducible tests, versioned control changes and recovery measures that show whether a newly hardened system actually reduces the identified risk.

The paper appeared in the May 2026 issue of IEEE Security & Privacy, and NIST summarized it publicly in June. NIST’s account says the long-run goal is to make finding new exploits more expensive than an attacker can justify, rather than promising absolute immunity.

The limits matter most where model actions can affect accounts, infrastructure, medical workflows or other high-consequence systems. A lower-risk assistant and an autonomous tool with privileged access should not receive identical monitoring budgets simply because both use generative AI.

The useful takeaway is narrower than the headline risk: fixed guardrails remain necessary, but they are not a finished security program. Deployment must include an operating loop for finding, patching and containing failures that were not visible when the original controls were written.

articles.body:
Five squares of fabric—each four inches on a side, some dyed and some undyed—are the center of a National Institute of Standards and Technology experiment in making textile sorting more measurable.

The set is Research Grade Test Material 10279, Textiles for Feedstock Identification. NIST developed it as a common object that laboratories, recyclers and manufacturers can scan with their own equipment, then use to compare how reliably different systems identify fibers.

That comparison matters because textile sorting is increasingly a machine-learning and measurement problem. Clothing can be labeled incorrectly, contain blended fibers or arrive too worn for a tag to settle the question. If one facility's scanner calls a swatch cotton and another reads the same material differently, automated sorting cannot produce a predictable feedstock.

A common method is near-infrared spectroscopy. A handheld or conveyor-mounted sensor shines near-infrared light on fabric and records how the material absorbs or scatters it. The resulting spectrum acts like a molecular fingerprint. Classification software then compares that signal with known examples to infer fiber content.

NIST says facilities also use computer vision, which sorts by color and visible appearance, and hyperspectral systems that combine imaging with spectral measurements. The new material is meant to test the measurement layer beneath those tools, not to declare one sorting architecture the winner.

RGTM 10279 contains five fabric types. NIST has deliberately withheld their fiber composition while participating laboratories analyze the squares. That blind structure is the point: researchers can compare reported results without telling participants the answer in advance.

Research Grade Test Materials are faster, more exploratory cousins of NIST's fully characterized standard reference materials. Laboratories receive them in exchange for measurements and feedback that help the agency decide whether the candidate is fit for purpose and what a better-characterized successor should contain.

The agency's study runs through Sept. 30. Its initial free-order window closed July 30. NIST says the results supplied by participating organizations will remain anonymous and will feed into development of a more thoroughly analyzed reference material.

The project also connects physical standards to open data. In March, NIST released NIR-SORT 2.0, an expanded public dataset of near-infrared spectra for textiles. A shared dataset helps researchers train and test classifiers; a shared physical sample lets them check whether instruments and methods agree on the same material in the real world.

NIST researchers say the benchmark could eventually help with production quality control, detecting fiber blends not reported on labels and assessing AI-assisted sorting. They also noted a possible use in fashion authentication, while explicitly saying that authentication is not part of their current work.

The immediate claim is narrower than the supply-chain promise. RGTM 10279 is a candidate under evaluation, not a certified fix for textile waste. The study has not yet published performance results, and NIST has not quantified how much the material might improve sorting accuracy, recycling volume or costs.

articles.body:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology plans an initial $20 million investment in a new center intended to move quantum hardware from specialized laboratory builds toward repeatable manufacturing.

Under an agreement announced June 29, SRI will establish the Quantum Manufacturing Extension Center. NIST said the center will focus on scalable, high-performance components and systems rather than selecting one winning quantum-computing architecture.

Quantum manufacturing has a different bottleneck from proving that a device can work once. Components must be produced with sufficiently consistent dimensions, materials and interfaces that performance survives across many units and through assembly into a larger system.

The center’s scope includes enabling infrastructure. NIST specifically pointed to cryostats, which maintain extremely low temperatures for some quantum devices, and lasers used to prepare, control or measure quantum states. Those tools can be as consequential to scale as the qubits or sensors themselves.

SRI is expected to convene developers, manufacturers and users around shared production problems. That model can expose gaps that a single laboratory may not see, including unavailable suppliers, incompatible specifications, slow test cycles and the absence of trusted measurement methods.

The effort builds on the Quantum Economic Development Consortium, a NIST-supported public-private partnership that began in 2019. QED-C participants include technology developers and prospective end users, giving the new center a network through which to identify manufacturing priorities.

The announcement is a capacity-building decision, not evidence that mass-produced quantum computers are imminent. NIST did not publish a factory-opening date, unit-cost target or production forecast, and different quantum technologies require different materials and operating environments.

The $20 million figure is also framed as an initial planned investment. It should not be treated as the center’s lifetime budget or as money already converted into equipment and commercial products.

The strategic bet is that shared manufacturing knowledge can shorten the distance between a research result and a reliable product. Success will be visible not only in faster devices, but in reproducible processes, qualified suppliers and measurements that let buyers compare whether components meet their claims.

A prototype carrier nicknamed the “coral torpedo” helped NOAA divers move lab-reared corals into the dim middle-light zone of the Gulf this spring, where the team planted 26 specimens on artificial reef structures at a depth of 66 meters, or about 217 feet.

The operation aboard NOAA Ship Nancy Foster combined laboratory propagation, specialized diving and new delivery hardware in an effort to rebuild mesophotic coral communities injured by the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill.

NOAA Fisheries reported the mission July 23. It said divers also relocated 16 coral fragments in the field to start new colonies—the first time rebreather divers had propagated these corals underwater and the first time divers had outplanted lab-reared mesophotic corals.

Corals previously traveled on large weighted “elevators” that resisted the water and were cumbersome to maneuver. The new streamlined tube, developed by NOAA fisheries biologist Chris Gardner, held prepared fragments and descended rapidly to a precise site where divers could remove and place them.

Speed matters because transported corals must move through changing water conditions without unnecessary mixing or handling. At depth, human divers could fit the small bases attached to the specimens into their intended positions on dome-shaped concrete structures.

The team completed decompression dives reaching 72.5 meters, or 237 feet. Closed-circuit rebreathers recycled breathing gas and extended bottom time, while a safety team and hyperbaric physician supported the operation.

Three soft-coral species were part of the planting work: Swiftia exserta, Muricea pendula and Thesea nivea. Mesophotic ecosystems live below shallow reefs but still receive some light, and they provide habitat that supports the Gulf food web.

NOAA said the crew collected 48 sediment cores and 51 live biological samples, sampled 11 colonies without removing them, mapped more than 14 square nautical miles of seafloor and collected water for organic-matter and environmental-DNA analysis.

The team also deployed three hydrophones to study whether habitat sound correlates with coral settlement and recorded stereo-camera surveys that can help researchers compare wild colony size with laboratory specimens.

Those measurements are the baseline for the harder question: whether the transplanted and newly propagated colonies survive and grow. NOAA has not yet reported long-term survival rates from this mission and says monitoring will continue.

The expedition is part of the Mesophotic and Deep Benthic Communities restoration portfolio led by NOAA for the Deepwater Horizon Open Ocean Trustee Implementation Group. A successful planting is a milestone, but ecological recovery will be measured over years rather than one voyage.

NOAA forecasts that the Gulf’s low-oxygen “dead zone” will cover about 7,027 square miles this summer, an area above the long-term measured average but below the record set nine years ago.

The estimate is roughly 1,804 square miles larger than the 39-year average of 5,223. It remains below the 8,776-square-mile record measured in 2017.

A dead zone forms when dissolved oxygen near the seafloor becomes too low to support much marine life. Nutrients carried through the Mississippi–Atchafalaya watershed stimulate algal growth; when the algae die and decompose, the process consumes oxygen.

The 2026 inputs do not all point in the same direction. Combined Mississippi and Atchafalaya discharge in May was about 36% below the 1980–2025 average, while nitrate load was 4% above average and phosphorus load 6% below.

Those numbers show why river volume alone does not determine the outcome. Nutrient concentration, delivery timing, winds, currents, temperature and water-column mixing can all affect how much low-oxygen water develops and persists.

USGS supplies the river measurements used by NOAA’s forecast models. The monitoring network includes about 2,972 real-time streamgages, 92 real-time nitrate sensors and 37 long-term sites across the watershed.

NOAA combines several models into an ensemble forecast. This is the ninth year it has produced the estimate that way, using different model structures to reduce dependence on any single projection.

The forecast is not the final area. A NOAA-supported summer cruise will measure the hypoxic zone directly, with results expected in early August. Weather and ocean conditions between the river-loading period and the survey can move the observed number above or below the model estimate.

The interagency task force’s long-term goal is 1,900 square miles by 2035. Against that benchmark, even an accurate 7,027-square-mile forecast would leave the system far from the target and keep nutrient reduction—not forecasting precision alone—at the center of the policy challenge.

bodyBlocks.text: NOAA forecasts that the Gulf’s low-oxygen “dead zone” will cover about 7,027 square miles this summer, an area above the long-term measured average but below the record set nine years ago.
The estimate is roughly 1,804 square miles larger than the 39-year average of 5,223. It remains below the 8,776-square-mile record measured in 2017.

A dead zone forms when dissolved oxygen near the seafloor becomes too low to support much marine life. Nutrients carried through the Mississippi–Atchafalaya watershed stimulate algal growth; when the algae die and decompose, the process consumes oxygen.

articles.body:
NOAA recorded 374 preliminary tornado reports across the United States in June, with Illinois, Indiana and Missouri each posting a state record for the month in an unusually active stretch of Midwest severe weather.

Illinois accounted for 91 preliminary reports, Indiana 69 and Missouri 32, according to the National Centers for Environmental Information’s June climate assessment using Storm Prediction Center data. The national number is a report count, not yet a final tornado count.

Multiple observers can report the same tornado, and later damage surveys may merge reports or revise event classifications. “Preliminary” is therefore essential: the figure measures the early operational record before NOAA completes its event-level reconciliation.

The severe-weather month occurred alongside broad warmth. The contiguous United States averaged 70.6°F in June, 2.2°F above the 20th-century average and within the warmest third of the 132-year national record.

Precipitation averaged 3.23 inches across the contiguous states, 0.31 inch above the 20th-century average and also in the wettest third of the record. Kansas, Illinois, Indiana and Kentucky ranked among their 10 wettest Junes.

National averages obscure the split geography. The West and Southwest completed their warmest January-through-June period on record while receiving less than 70% of normal precipitation. Several western states had only about half to two-thirds of average precipitation.

The East also contained dry pockets: nine states from South Carolina through Massachusetts ranked among their eight driest first halves of a year. At the same time, parts of the Midwest and Great Lakes were notably wet, and Michigan had its wettest January–June on record.

Drought covered less than half of the contiguous United States by the end of June, but persisted across much of the interior West and developed in Puerto Rico. A smaller national drought footprint does not mean every region improved.

The report is a climate accounting, not a local forecast or warning. Its value is in separating the pieces: preliminary severe-weather reports, measured monthly averages and regional rankings that show how one wet and stormy month can coexist with persistent western heat and dryness.

articles.body:
NOAA is moving the high-performance computing behind its operational weather forecast models to commercial cloud infrastructure, with Google Cloud supporting National Weather Service systems under a transition announced July 27.

The change centers on the Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System, the computing environment used to run numerical models that turn observations and physical equations into forecast guidance.

NOAA says the new architecture should be more flexible and easier to update. Commercial cloud capacity can be provisioned differently from fixed agency-owned machines, potentially giving model teams more options when testing or scaling workloads.

The announcement does not quantify a forecast-accuracy gain, cost savings or a final migration date. Those omissions matter because a platform change is an infrastructure decision, not evidence that every resulting forecast will immediately improve.

Forecast skill depends on more than processors. Satellites, radar, surface stations, balloons, buoys and aircraft supply observations. Data-assimilation systems combine those inputs, numerical models calculate possible atmospheric states, and forecasters interpret guidance for local products and warnings.

Cloud computing changes the model-run layer of that chain. It does not replace observation networks or National Weather Service forecast offices, and it does not remove scientific uncertainty from predicting a chaotic atmosphere.

Operational reliability will be central. Weather guidance runs on strict schedules, and missed delivery windows can reduce the value of even a sophisticated model. NOAA will need capacity, network performance, security and continuity controls that support recurring national workloads.

Update speed is another test. Forecast systems evolve through new physics, data sources, resolution and software. NOAA’s stated goal of an easier-to-update environment will be meaningful only if validated changes can move into operations without sacrificing reproducibility or uptime.

The public should therefore judge the transition by evidence released after migration: stable model cycles, documented upgrades, latency, cost, outage handling and independently measured forecast skill.

The immediate news is narrower but consequential. NOAA is changing the computing foundation beneath national weather prediction, choosing commercial cloud support for a workload that feeds daily forecasts and warnings across the country.

articles.body:
NOAA’s latest week-two hazards outlook places three very different risks on the same national map: extreme heat across much of the South, heavy monsoon rain in the Southwest and the possibility of rapid-onset drought in parts of the Plains and Mississippi Valley.

The Climate Prediction Center product, issued Aug. 5 for the period Aug. 13 through Aug. 19, is a regional risk assessment rather than a day-by-day local forecast. It highlights where forecast models and recent conditions support elevated concern eight to 14 days ahead.

A moderate risk of extreme heat covers parts of the Southern and Central Plains and the Lower Mississippi Valley for Aug. 12 through Aug. 15. A wider slight-risk area extends across much of the south-central United States, Southeast and Mid-Atlantic through Aug. 18.

NOAA tied the heat risk to persistent high pressure and humid air moving north from the Gulf. Its combined GEFS and ECMWF tool showed at least a 40% chance across broad areas that maximum temperature or heat index would exceed the local 90th percentile at some point during the period.

The strongest modeled signal reached as high as 70% in parts of the Lower Mississippi Valley. Those probabilities describe conditions relative to local climate, not a single temperature threshold shared by every city.

The outlook discontinued an earlier heat-risk area for the Intermountain West and Northern Plains as models increasingly favored a West Coast trough and moderating temperatures there. Forecast confidence was higher in the southern heat signal than in earlier runs, the discussion said.

The same developing western trough may help draw more moisture into the Southwest monsoon. NOAA posted a moderate risk of heavy precipitation for parts of the Desert Southwest and southern Great Basin from Aug. 12 through Aug. 14, with a broader slight-risk area lasting through Aug. 18.

Model ensembles showed widespread chances above 50% for three-day precipitation totals to exceed half an inch in parts of the region, with smaller areas carrying a 20% chance of more than one inch. In dry washes and canyons, relatively modest totals can still produce flash flooding.

A separate slight-risk area for heavy precipitation covers parts of the Great Lakes, Ohio Valley and Upper Mississippi Valley early in the period. NOAA said humid air and possible mesoscale convective systems could support intense rainfall, while acknowledging that models disagreed on the evolving upper-level pattern.

Parts of the Central and Southern Plains, the Ozarks and the Lower and Middle Mississippi Valley carry a rapid-onset drought designation. NOAA cited 30-day precipitation deficits greater than two inches in portions of that area, along with continued heat and dryness into mid-August.

Rapid-onset drought is not simply a long dry spell. It describes deterioration that accelerates over weeks as limited rain combines with high temperatures, wind and atmospheric demand for moisture. The risk designation signals favorable conditions for that process; it does not certify that every county inside the boundary will enter drought.

Because the product looks more than a week ahead, exact hazard boundaries and timing can shift. NOAA directs readers to local National Weather Service offices for short-range, location-specific forecasts and warnings.

The larger lesson is visible in the map’s contrasts. A stronger monsoon can raise flash-flood risk in the Southwest while persistent heat and rainfall deficits worsen soil moisture farther east. National weather does not move as one condition, even within the same forecast week.

articles.body:
The National Science Foundation awarded $83 million for a new layer of research infrastructure intended to connect scientific datasets with computing systems and artificial-intelligence tools, rather than leaving researchers to assemble those links project by project.

The Integrated Data Systems and Services program includes two awards for national-scale systems. Fabric for AI-Driven Science, led by the Morgridge Institute for Research, will build a data fabric connecting repositories and computing resources. The National Data Platform, led by UC San Diego, will integrate distributed data, facilities and AI resources.

Four more projects are moving toward national operations. UCLA’s Interactive Discovery Laboratory will offer browser-based access to computing and data; UC Irvine’s BRIDGE will support reusable workflows; Tennessee’s National Science Data Fabric will connect distributed data; and Arizona’s MESA will use metadata automation to organize cross-disciplinary datasets.

NSF also issued planning grants for future infrastructure proposals. The announcement reports an $83 million portfolio total but does not imply that each project received an equal share.

The technical goal is interoperability: data, instruments, software, models and computing resources should be discoverable and usable together. That matters for AI research because large models and automated workflows require data with enough metadata, access controls and consistency to be reused reliably.

The agency frames the awards as complementary to the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource and other cyberinfrastructure investments. In that architecture, computing capacity is only one layer; researchers also need stable paths to the data that trains, tests or feeds scientific models.

Reproducibility is another stated target. Shared platforms can preserve workflows and make it easier for a second team to find the same data and rerun an analysis, although software versions, permissions and discipline-specific standards still affect whether replication succeeds.

The award announcement describes intended capabilities, not completed national services. The named institutions must still build, integrate and operate the systems, attract users and demonstrate that distributed data can move through the proposed workflows without creating new bottlenecks.

If implementation works, the practical change will be mundane but consequential: scientists should spend less time locating, cleaning and moving data between incompatible systems, and more time testing questions with traceable inputs and reusable methods.
