articles.body:
The World Bank has approved $375.9 million for equipment intended to stabilize Pakistan’s transmission grid and move wind power that existing bottlenecks keep from reaching customers.

The financing, approved July 9, covers the first phase of a 10-year program called Boosting Energy Security through Transmission in Pakistan, or BEST-PAK. Its immediate engineering focus is voltage control at high-capacity substations rather than construction of a new wind farm.

World Bank estimates say the upgrades can unlock 640 megawatts of wind generation now being curtailed and enable the full use of 1,840 megawatts of wind capacity in southern Pakistan. Those are project objectives, not power already delivered by newly installed equipment.

Plans call for static synchronous compensators, known as STATCOMs, at three major 500-kilovolt substations. These power-electronics systems inject or absorb reactive power quickly, helping operators keep grid voltage within limits when supply and demand change.

Fixed reactors and capacitor banks are planned across 26 additional substations. Reactors can absorb reactive power when voltage is too high; capacitor banks can supply it when voltage is too low. Together, the devices address stability limits that can force operators to reduce generation even when turbines are available.

The project is also designed to make room for about 491 megawatts of planned private-sector renewable projects. Whether all of that capacity is built and connected depends on decisions beyond this World Bank financing.

Pakistan has committed to a 60% renewable share in its electricity mix by 2030 under its climate plan. The grid project can support that goal, but it does not by itself guarantee the target, determine future demand or resolve every financial problem in the power sector.

The physical specifications respond to two hazards that can disable substations: flooding and heat. New installations are to use elevated platforms where flood exposure demands it, and equipment must be rated to operate at temperatures up to 55 degrees Celsius, or 131 degrees Fahrenheit.

Those standards matter because transmission equipment loses performance and ages faster when temperatures exceed its design envelope. Elevation can protect critical gear from inundation, but it cannot eliminate every flood risk to access roads, communications or connected lines.

The World Bank estimates the project could avoid about 832,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide a year, or more than 20.8 million tons over 25 years. That is a modeled impact. It depends on the upgrades being completed, wind power displacing more carbon-intensive generation and the grid operating as assumed.

BEST-PAK is framed as more than an equipment purchase. The first phase also supports Pakistan’s plan to restructure the National Transmission & Dispatch Company into specialized successor organizations and strengthen governance and operating performance.

Institutional reform introduces its own execution risk. Dividing responsibilities can clarify accountability, but only if staffing, control-room authority, maintenance budgets, data and emergency procedures remain coordinated across the new entities.

The approval is therefore a financing milestone, not completion evidence. Procurement, installation, commissioning and measured reductions in curtailment will determine whether the project produces its advertised capacity and reliability gains.

The most useful public checks will be operational: which substations receive equipment, when each system enters service, how often wind is still curtailed and whether voltage and outage indicators improve. Until those data arrive, the World Bank figures are a detailed plan with explicit engineering targets.

The World Bank approved a $1.02 billion financing package tied to energy and water reforms in the Philippines, pairing a large policy loan with a performance grant and targets for renewable power, offshore wind and local water utilities.

The Second Energy Transition and Climate Resilience Development Policy Loan consists of a $1 billion loan from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and a $20 million performance-based grant from the Livable Planet Fund.

Unlike a construction loan assigned to one plant or pipeline, development-policy financing supports an agreed package of policy and institutional actions. The announced measures include operating the Renewable Energy Market, incorporating electric-vehicle charging into utility planning and launching the country’s first offshore-wind auction.

That auction targets 3.3 gigawatts of contracted offshore-wind capacity by 2030. The World Bank said the broader reforms are expected to mobilize about $7 billion in private investment, a forecast that depends on investors responding to the new market rules.

The energy target is specific: renewables would rise from 30% to 42% of installed generating capacity by 2027. Installed capacity is not the same as electricity actually generated, because output varies by technology, weather, fuel availability and plant use.

The operation also addresses local water services. More than 1,600 local government units are responsible for provision, according to the World Bank, but many lack financing or institutional capacity. The reforms support cost-recovery tariff frameworks, a unified financing structure and bulk-water pricing regulations.

By 2027, the program aims to expand the number of local water providers with sustainable business plans from 10 to 100. The financing structure is designed to prioritize poor and climate-vulnerable communities, but the announcement does not list every provider that will qualify.

The policy loan builds on an earlier operation that established a legal framework for offshore wind, launched a reserve market, expanded retail-energy competition and created institutional groundwork for more sustainable local water service.

The numbers should be read as different categories: $1.02 billion is the approved public financing package; roughly $7 billion is expected private mobilization; 42% is a 2027 installed-capacity target; and 3.3 gigawatts is the offshore-wind auction goal for 2030. Delivery will depend on implementation beyond the approval itself.

articles.body:
More than 1,700 young athletes from more than 135 countries are due at Hayward Field this week for the World Athletics U20 Championships, a five-day meet that opens Wednesday with three distance finals, the men’s shot put and a mixed 4-by-400-meter relay.

The Aug. 5–9 championships are the 21st edition of the global under-20 meet and the second staged in Oregon. The last Oregon edition was held at the former Hayward Field in 2014; the rebuilt stadium later hosted the 2022 senior world championships.

World Athletics’ most recent event release gives the expected scale as more than 1,700 athletes from more than 135 countries. Those are organizer figures, not a final count of starters: accreditation, travel and late withdrawals can change the field before each event.

The first champion is scheduled to come from the men’s shot put at 7:50 p.m. local time Wednesday. The women’s and men’s 5,000-meter finals follow, and the mixed 4-by-400 closes the opening session at 8:50 p.m.

The women’s and men’s 100-meter finals anchor Thursday evening. Friday concentrates on qualifying and combined-events competition. World Athletics lists 12 finals for Saturday evening and 15 titles on Sunday, when the championships end with the women’s and men’s 4-by-400 relays.

One new feature is the mixed 4-by-100-meter relay. World Athletics’ published program places its first round Thursday morning and the final Saturday evening. The mixed 4-by-400 remains on the opening-night schedule.

The U20 championships sit at an unusual point in the sport. The competition awards world titles, but the field spans athletes whose bodies, coaching environments and experience are still changing quickly. A standout performance can signal elite potential without guaranteeing a senior career.

That makes restraint important in covering the meet. Boho News will report verified results and competition records without turning teenage athletes into permanent projections or publishing unnecessary personal details. Athlete eligibility and official result lists remain the governing sources.

The event’s medals use the same geometric tree-and-wings form as the Oregon 26 logo. Organizers describe the tree as a reference to the state’s landscape and the wings as a link to the winged-foot symbol of track and field and Oregon’s “She flies with her own wings” motto.

Ribbon colors distinguish the medals: blue for gold, red and orange for silver, and green for bronze. Podium athletes are also due to receive matching pins intended for a coach, family member, friend or teammate.

Published schedules are operational documents, not guarantees. Heat assignments, advancement, weather and competition appeals can alter the order or timing. The official World Athletics timetable and results system should be checked immediately before any event or result is reported.

The reliable opening-day frame is broader: a five-day global junior championship returns to Eugene, introduces a mixed sprint relay to the U20 program and begins awarding titles immediately. The results from Hayward Field—not pre-meet projections—will determine which athletes leave with the new Oregon-shaped medals.

articles.body:
Global merchandise trade remained above its recent trend in the first half of 2026, but the World Trade Organization’s latest leading indicator shows momentum beginning to cool.

The WTO Goods Trade Barometer registered 101.7, down from 102.3 in January. Because 100 is the indicator’s trend baseline, the new reading points to above-trend trade volume with a weaker signal than at the start of the year.

The number is not a growth percentage. The barometer combines several forward-looking measures to show direction relative to recent trends; it does not mean world trade grew 1.7% or guarantee that the next quarterly volume report will match the signal.

Electronic components were the clear outlier at 105.5. The WTO connected that strength to demand associated with artificial-intelligence investment, which helped offset other pressure on trade during the first half of the year.

Transport measures still pointed to expansion. Container shipping stood at 102.4 and air freight at 102.2, although the WTO said both were expanding more slowly than a few months earlier. Export orders were only slightly above trend at 100.5.

Two goods-producing components were below the baseline: agricultural raw materials at 98.9 and automotive products at 99.8. The mix describes resilience rather than synchronized acceleration across every part of the trading system.

The WTO’s separate March outlook projected merchandise-trade growth of 1.9% in 2026 under its baseline and 1.4% in a high-energy-price scenario. It said sustained AI investment could add 0.5 percentage points, a scenario contribution rather than growth already booked.

The organization also noted that importers accelerated purchases before anticipated tariff increases in early 2025. That timing boosted year-over-year growth before it slowed later in the year, complicating comparisons with 2026.

The next trade forecast is scheduled for October. Until then, the barometer’s message is carefully bounded: world goods trade is holding above trend, electronics are doing unusual work in the index, and the aggregate signal is softer than it was in January.

articles.body:
The Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden will reopen its renovated outdoor space this fall with three new monumental heads by Yoshitomo Nara, beginning an annual series of artist commissions on the museum’s West Lawn.

“Yoshitomo Nara: Sentinels of Stillness” is scheduled to run from Oct. 31, 2026, through Nov. 7, 2027, the Smithsonian announced Tuesday. The presentation will bring “Long Tall Peace Sister,” “Smiling” and “Tiny Bright Round Eyes,” all dated 2025, to the National Mall.

Each work enlarges a palm-sized clay head Nara made in 2021. The finished sculptures are fabricated in aluminum and coated in white urethane paint, translating the irregularity of hand-shaped clay into forms intended for an outdoor public setting.

Hirshhorn Director Melissa Chiu said the show will establish a yearly West Lawn exhibition by a leading international artist. Anne Reeve, a Hirshhorn curator, organized the first installment, which the museum says will include free tours and art education.

The announcement describes the three heads as evoking childhood snowdrifts and as emphasizing how daylight changes across their surfaces. Those are the museum’s and artist’s interpretive frames; visitors will not be able to evaluate the installed works until the garden opens.

The new series is separate from the Hirshhorn’s permanent collection. The first show has a defined closing date in November 2027, and the museum says a different commissioned artist will follow on the lawn each year.

Nara’s sculpture practice predates the new works by decades. He began making figurative wood carvings in the mid-1980s, later worked with fiber-reinforced plastic, lacquer and urethane, and developed his ceramic practice during a 2007 residency in Shigaraki, Japan.

According to the Hirshhorn, Nara turned more deeply to hand-molded clay after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and Fukushima nuclear disaster affected his home region. He conceived large-scale sculptural enlargements in 2020 and made the small heads behind the new trio the following year.

The museum’s account is biographical, not a claim that the new works document the disaster. The announced sculptures are presented as contemporary public art shaped by material process, memory and scale.

The sculpture garden closed for renovation in 2023. Its redesign by Hiroshi Sugimoto received approvals from the Commission of Fine Arts and the National Capital Planning Commission in 2022 after public consultation.

The Smithsonian says the reopening will add an expanded entrance from the National Mall and refresh the passage connecting the garden with the museum building and plaza. Those access changes matter because the original 1974 sunken design could be difficult to enter and navigate.

The museum has not attached a separate ticket price to the exhibition. The Hirshhorn’s public programs and galleries are free, although operating details can change before the Oct. 31 opening.

For now, the firm facts are the artists, titles, dates, materials and planned series. The appearance of the completed installation, its relationship to the redesigned lawn and the visitor experience remain future-facing until the site reopens.
